sections.title: Customer Identification and Segmentation
sections.summary: All quality begins with identifying who the customer is — internal vs external, primary vs secondary vs indirect, B2B vs B2C. Customers are segmented by volume, profitability, industry, geography, demographics, or psychographics. Qualitative data (opinions, beliefs) and quantitative data (counts, measurements) both inform decisions, with the right type chosen for the question being asked.

concepts.definition: (1) Primary — directly receives process output; (2) Secondary — receives output but is not the process's reason for being; (3) Indirect — affected by but does not receive output directly; (4) External — end user/consumer; (5) False — performs activities that do not add value; (6) Internal — next operation/function within the organization.
concepts.examTip: Especially distinguish primary, secondary, indirect, and false customers.

concepts.definition: Every function and process within the organization is both a receiver and provider — 'next operation as customer' (Bhote). Treating internal customers well cascades to external customer satisfaction.
concepts.examTip: Internal customer is foundational to TQM. Poor internal treatment → poor external service.

concepts.definition: Internal service agreements between provider and receiver. Three timely tenets: (1) requirements meet receiver needs, (2) measurement is consistent with needs, (3) internal requirements align with external customer requirements.
concepts.examTip: QLAs make internal expectations explicit and measurable.

concepts.term: Seven Steps to Improve Internal Customer Interfaces
concepts.definition: (1) Identify interfaces; (2) Assess gaps; (3) Set objectives & measurements; (4) Feasibility study of changes; (5) Modify processes; (6) Track and report; (7) Document QLAs.
concepts.examTip: Step 1 (identify interfaces) is most often skipped — easy to assume you already know.

concepts.definition: Wholesale buyer, Distributor, Retail chain buyer, Other volume buyers (gov't, education, healthcare), Retail buyer, Discount buyer, Employee buyer, Service buyer, Service user, Organization buyer.
concepts.examTip: Each type has distinct influence on design, pricing, packaging, and delivery.

concepts.definition: B2C: provider sells directly to consumers — straightforward to capture VOC. B2B: 'real customer' is often unclear; multiple stakeholders in purchasing decision; each stakeholder group has unique requirements.
concepts.examTip: B2B requires segmenting by stakeholder role within the buying organization.

concepts.definition: Purchase volume, profitability, industry, type of purchases, type of organization, geographic, demographic (age, income, gender), psychographic (lifestyle, attitudes), buyers' organizational structure.
concepts.examTip: Profitability segmentation is more useful than volume — high-volume customers may not be profitable.

concepts.definition: (1) Homogeneous — all customers have similar preferences (compete in middle); (2) Diffused — no natural segments, varied preferences; (3) Clustered — distinct natural groups (target with cluster analysis).
concepts.examTip: Clustered preferences enable targeted marketing — most actionable for segmentation.

concepts.definition: Core customer segment representing the most strategic value. Avoid the trap of treating all customers as equally important — bar set too low for core customers means delivering minimum to everyone.
concepts.examTip: Pareto applies to customers — focus on vital few without abandoning the rest.

concepts.term: 8-Step Process for Working with External Customers
concepts.definition: (1) Define & prioritize segments; (2) Capture VOC for key segments (gap analysis); (3) Identify required internal process changes; (4) Action plans; (5) Risk analysis; (6) Test market; (7) Roll out; (8) Evaluate effectiveness.
concepts.examTip: Step 5 (risk analysis) and Step 6 (test market) are commonly skipped.

concepts.definition: Qualitative: subjective — opinions, beliefs, feelings, attitudes (interviews, focus groups, observation, content analysis). Quantitative: objective — counts, measurements, statistical estimates (surveys with closed questions, transactional data).
concepts.examTip: Qualitative explores WHY; quantitative measures HOW MUCH/MANY.

concepts.definition: One-on-one interviews (in-person/phone/mystery shoppers), focus groups, observation of behavior, content analysis of memos/comments, surveys with open-ended questions for in-depth exploration.
concepts.examTip: Open-ended surveys + interviews are the highest-quality qualitative inputs.

concepts.definition: (1) Analyze raw data — rank, correlate, segment, compare to past; (2) Compare findings to other internal/external data; (3) Communicate to decision-makers; (4) Use the information and verify results with follow-up.
concepts.examTip: Follow-up surveys after improvements close the loop.

keyFigures: Sam Walton ('there is only one boss—the customer')

practiceQuestions.q: An inspector who 100% checks every part because of historical deficiencies is BEST classified as a:
practiceQuestions.explanation: A false customer performs activities that do not add value. The 100% inspection persists because of past failures, not because it adds value to the end product.

practiceQuestions.q: Which segmentation criterion is BEST for prioritizing strategic customer focus?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Profitability-based segmentation reveals which customers actually generate value. Volume alone can be misleading — high-volume customers may erode margins.

practiceQuestions.q: Quality-Level Agreements (QLAs) are MOST appropriate for:
practiceQuestions.explanation: QLAs (also called SLAs internally) formalize service expectations between internal providers and receivers. They cascade external requirements into internal commitments.

practiceQuestions.q: Open-ended interview questions are BEST suited to gather:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Open-ended questions surface qualitative insights — beliefs, motivations, attitudes. Quantitative data comes from closed questions and transactional sources.

flashcards.back: Primary, Secondary, Indirect, External, False, Internal.
An individual or group performing non-value-added activities (e.g., 100% inspector compensating for poor process).
B2B has multiple stakeholders in the buying decision; the 'real customer' is often unclear.
Qualitative = subjective (opinions, beliefs). Quantitative = objective (counts, measurements).

sections.title: Customer Relationship Management
sections.summary: CRM coordinates all customer touchpoints to learn about needs, build retention, and grow loyalty. Key tools: VOC capture, QFD (House of Quality), Kano Model (must-be / one-dimensional / attractive / indifferent / reverse), NPS, complaint handling, and the five-step service recovery process. Modern focus: customer experience management across the full journey.

concepts.definition: Strategy and toolset to learn customers' needs, values, and behaviors; segment them; coordinate sales, service, and marketing information across all touchpoints. Most-advanced form: partnerships and alliances.
concepts.examTip: CRM ≠ a software tool. It's the strategy; software supports it.

concepts.definition: Customer-focused: emphasizes care and retention of EXISTING customers. Market-driven: emphasizes attracting NEW customers. Both are needed, but quality management leans customer-focused.
concepts.examTip: Retention is cheaper than acquisition (Reichheld). Quality programs prioritize customer-focused.

concepts.definition: System for systematically capturing what customers want/need and how well current products/services meet expectations. Inputs: complaints, surveys, listening posts, focus groups, mystery shoppers, social media. Outputs: requirements, satisfaction scores, improvement priorities.
concepts.examTip: VOC is a SYSTEM, not a single survey. Multiple touchpoints feed it.

concepts.definition: Methodology translating customer voice (qualitative requirements) into operational requirements using a series of matrices (House of Quality). Cascades through 4 levels: Customer Requirements → Design → Parts → Process → Production.
concepts.examTip: QFD is heavily tested. Know all 4 cascading levels.

concepts.definition: Sections: (A) Customer wants/needs (VOC); (B) Importance weighting; (C) Customer perception of competitors; (D) Critical process characteristics (Voice of Company); (E) Relationship strength matrix; (F) Importance rating; (G) Correlations (the 'roof'); (H) Targets.
concepts.examTip: Memorize sections A–H. Roof (G) shows relationships among technical characteristics.

concepts.term: Kano Model — Five Quality Element Categories
concepts.definition: (1) Must-be (basic — dissatisfaction if absent, no satisfaction if present); (2) One-dimensional (linear — satisfaction scales with fulfillment); (3) Attractive/Delighters (unexpected features that delight); (4) Indifferent (no impact either way); (5) Reverse (some users dissatisfied when feature is provided).
concepts.examTip: HEAVILY TESTED. Yesterday's delighters become today's must-be's (e.g., automobile cup holders).

concepts.definition: Must-be: lower-right curve (saturates at neutral). One-dimensional: straight diagonal line. Attractive: upper-left curve (rises rapidly with fulfillment). Indifferent: flat horizontal line. Reverse: opposite of expected.
concepts.examTip: Visualize the curves — must-be saturates; attractive accelerates.

concepts.definition: Formal process for capturing casual/informal customer remarks. ICALL (Informal Customer Acquisition Listening and Learning) formalizes the practice. Captures suggestions, displeasures, ideas, and signals of customer departure.
concepts.examTip: Listening posts catch what surveys miss — early warning of customer issues.

concepts.definition: Written/mail (30–50% response), telephone (higher response, faster), in-person (most powerful but expensive), e-mail/web (cheapest, variable response), comment cards, mystery shopping, social media monitoring, joint planning meetings, customer panels, advisory councils.
concepts.examTip: Match method to objective: in-person for depth, web for breadth, mystery shopping for service consistency.

concepts.definition: 9.5% of non-complainers (with >$100 loss) repurchase. 19% of complainers with unresolved issues repurchase. 54.3% repurchase when complaint is resolved — and even higher with quick resolution.
concepts.examTip: Resolving complaints quickly is the highest-leverage retention tool.

concepts.definition: (1) Market-perceived quality profile; (2) Market-perceived price profile; (3) Customer value map; (4) Won/lost analysis; (5) Head-to-head area chart; (6) Key events timeline; (7) What/who matrix.
concepts.examTip: Gale & Wood's 7 tools — used to quantify customer-perceived value vs. competition.

concepts.definition: (1) Dissatisfied — departed; (2) Marginally satisfied — easily lost; (3) Basically satisfied — probably gone; (4) Delighted — returns (retained); (5) Committed advocate — loyal AND tells others.
concepts.examTip: 'Basically satisfied' is NOT good — they often leave silently.

concepts.definition: Single question: 'How likely are you to recommend us?' on 0–10 scale. Promoters (9–10), Passives (7–8), Detractors (0–6).
concepts.examTip: NPS ranges from −100 to +100. Memorize the 9–10 / 7–8 / 0–6 thresholds.

concepts.definition: Total economic value of a customer over the entire relationship. Considers acquisition cost, base profit, revenue growth, operating costs, referrals, and price premium. Reichheld pioneered this measure.
concepts.examTip: Retention is cheaper than acquisition — CLV justifies retention investment.

concepts.definition: Mapping the cumulative impact of multiple touchpoints over the customer journey. Includes personas, key moments, positive/negative impacts, and emotions. Visual journey mapping is the core tool.
concepts.examTip: CXM ≠ CRM. CRM = data; CXM = end-to-end experience design.

concepts.definition: Risk to organizational reputation and customer goodwill. Damage translates to lost revenue, increased capital costs, and shareholder value destruction. Boeing 737 MAX example: FAA grounding caused billions in lost revenue and cancelled orders.
concepts.examTip: Reputational risk is now a top-3 ERM concern for most large organizations.

concepts.term: Six Critical Areas of Customer-Centric Organizations
concepts.definition: (1) Equip, enable, engage employees; (2) Leadership, vision, support; (3) Create & deploy service strategies; (4) Master service delivery processes; (5) Performance measurement (VOC); (6) Resource & infrastructure development.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 6 areas — exam may give a deficiency and ask which area it falls under.

concepts.definition: (1) Apologize sincerely and accept responsibility; (2) Restate to confirm understanding; (3) Empathize and commit to resolution; (4) Make Restitution (specific, tangible); (5) Follow Up to verify satisfaction.
concepts.examTip: Memorize all 5 steps in order. Skipping #5 (follow-up) loses the recovery effect.

concepts.definition: (1) Replace failed products at equal or refund value; (2) Re-do substandard service; (3) Customer not challenged; (4) Quick and fair settlement; (5) Sincere apology that restores loyalty.
concepts.examTip: Unconditional guarantees demonstrate confidence and build loyalty.

concepts.definition: Resolving conflicts among customers competing for resources requires understanding cost to produce/deliver, segment-specific needs, capacity planning, and prioritization aligned to strategy. Building long-term relationships often requires reducing supplier base.
concepts.examTip: Conflict resolution becomes a competitive advantage in the industry.

keyFigures: Bradley Gale & Robert Wood (Customer Value Analysis)
Fred Reichheld (Net Promoter Score, customer loyalty)

practiceQuestions.q: In the Kano Model, automobile cup holders today are MOST likely to be:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cup holders were delighters when introduced; over time customer expectations shifted them to must-be (their absence causes dissatisfaction; presence is expected).

practiceQuestions.q: An NPS survey returns 60% promoters, 25% passives, 15% detractors. The NPS is:
Which step in the five-step recovery process is MOST often skipped, eroding the recovery's effectiveness?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Follow-up — verifying that the customer is now satisfied — is the step most commonly omitted. Without it, the customer can't tell if the apology was sincere.

practiceQuestions.q: QFD cascades through how many primary levels?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Four levels: Customer Requirements → Design Requirements → Parts Requirements → Process Requirements (with Production controls).

practiceQuestions.q: A 'committed advocate' (Level 5 satisfaction) is BEST described as:
options: A customer who is satisfied with basic product features
A loyal customer who tells others
practiceQuestions.explanation: Level 5 = committed advocate. Loyal AND actively promotes — the highest tier.

flashcards.back: Customer Reqs → Design Reqs → Parts Reqs → Process Reqs.
Dissatisfied → Marginal → Basically satisfied → Delighted → Committed advocate.
Apologize → Restate → Empathize → Make Restitution → Follow Up.
Customer-focused = retain existing. Market-driven = attract new.
